vignette:
Marcus

Marcus is a 47-year-old bus driver who has spent nearly two decades navigating the same city routes, learning the rhythms of his passengers and the pulse of the streets. He describes his work as something he has always taken quiet pride in — the dependability of it, the way people count on him to get them somewhere safely. That sense of reliability has been one of the few constants holding his life together since the night, three years ago, when everything shifted.

It happened on a Friday evening after his shift. Marcus had pulled into a convenience store two blocks from his depot, a stop he made routinely. What followed unfolded in under four minutes, though he says it has never felt that short. Police responded to a reported disturbance nearby, and Marcus — tall, Black, wearing a dark jacket — was ordered to the ground at gunpoint before he had fully processed what was happening. He was shouted at, physically restrained, and held face-down on the pavement while officers sorted out the situation. No charges were filed. He was told he could go. No one apologized.

He drove home that night in a kind of numb disbelief. In the days that followed, he kept waiting to feel angry, or relieved, or something definitive. Instead, he found himself replaying the moment the first officer's voice hit him — that particular pitch of command — over and over, involuntarily, the way a song gets stuck. He started having trouble sleeping, lying awake with his heart beating too fast, certain something was about to go wrong without knowing what.

The intrusions moved into his working days. Certain sounds on his route — a radio crackling, someone shouting from the sidewalk, the flash of blue and red lights in his mirrors — could pull him back to the pavement so completely that he would lose several seconds of the present. He began gripping the steering wheel harder than he needed to. Passengers noticed he had become quieter, less likely to exchange the small jokes he used to offer at red lights.

Off the bus, Marcus has reorganized his life around avoidance in ways he rarely names directly. He no longer stops at that convenience store, or any in that neighborhood. He takes longer routes home. He has stopped attending the monthly card games he used to host at his apartment, finding the idea of having people over — the noise, the unpredictability — exhausting rather than pleasurable. A relationship he had been cautiously building with a woman he met through a friend quietly dissolved; he found himself unable to explain why he kept pulling back, only that closeness had started to feel like exposure.

He describes a persistent sense of being watched when he is outside on foot, a low-grade alertness that never fully powers down. He scans faces at bus stops and intersections with a vigilance he knows is excessive but cannot talk himself out of. Some mornings he sits in his parked bus before opening the doors, breathing slowly, preparing himself. He has not told his dispatcher or any of his coworkers what happened. He worries they would not understand, or worse, that they would minimize it the way the officers did — efficiently, without cruelty, as if his experience had no particular weight.

What Marcus returns to most often in conversation is not the fear he felt on the ground, but the moment after — being told he was free to go, and realizing that no one in that interaction had ever seen him as a person with somewhere to be, someone who was trusted daily with other people's lives and safety. He carries that realization the way he carries everything now: quietly, while still showing up for his route, while still getting people where they need to go, while the world outside his windshield continues to feel like a place that can turn on him without warning and offer no accounting for it afterward.
